# Row and Completeness Validations {#sec-row-validations}

```{python}
#| include: false
import pointblank as pb
pb.config(report_incl_header=False, report_incl_footer=False)
```

Column checks ask whether a value is acceptable. Row checks ask whether a whole row is acceptable,
and some problems only show up when you look at rows. A row can have a valid value in every column
and still be wrong, either because it duplicates another row or because a field it needs is empty.
To catch those problems, the row has to be the unit of validation rather than the individual cell.

This chapter covers the two row-level checks that come up most often: distinctness and
completeness. Most of the chapter is about the decisions each one involves. For distinctness, that
means choosing which columns make up the key. For completeness, it means deciding which fields are
required and which are optional. Both checks produce one test unit per row, so their reports read
like the per-row column checks of @sec-column-validations and tell you how many rows are affected.
Some other row-level checks, like rules that tie several columns together or judgments made by an
AI model, have their own chapters, and we point to those at the end.

We use `game_revenue` for realistic scale and the smaller `small_table` when a short result makes
the behavior easier to see.

```{python}
game_revenue = pb.load_dataset(dataset="game_revenue", tbl_type="polars")
small_table = pb.load_dataset(dataset="small_table", tbl_type="polars")
```

## Row distinctness

Duplicate rows cause trouble that is easy to miss. They inflate counts and averages, and they can
make later steps process the same record twice. They also usually point to a problem earlier in the
pipeline, such as a deduplication step that failed or a join that matched more rows than expected.
The `rows_distinct()` method finds duplicates, and most of the work in using it is deciding what
"duplicate" should mean.

### Checking whole-row uniqueness

With no arguments, `rows_distinct()` compares entire rows and checks that no two are identical
across every column. The `small_table` dataset has one exact duplicate, which the check finds.

```{python}
(
    pb.Validate(data=small_table)
    .rows_distinct()
    .interrogate()
)
```

Eleven of the 13 rows pass and two fail. The two failures are the identical pair (both dated
2016-01-20 04:30:00). Notice that both copies fail, not just the second one. Pointblank has no way
of knowing which copy is the original, and counting every copy gives you the full size of the
problem. A larger table can easily pass this whole-row check, as `game_revenue` does.

```{python}
(
    pb.Validate(data=game_revenue)
    .rows_distinct()
    .interrogate()
)
```

All 2,000 rows are distinct across the full set of columns, so the check passes. That does not mean
the table has no duplicates, though. Exact whole-row duplicates are the less common problem, and the
more useful check is on a key.

### Choosing the key

Usually you want uniqueness on a key, meaning a column or combination of columns that identifies a
record, and you want to ignore the other columns. The `columns_subset=` argument does this. The
choice of columns decides what the check means, and the wrong choice gives a result that is correct
but not useful. Using `session_id` alone as the key shows what that looks like.

```{python}
(
    pb.Validate(data=game_revenue)
    .rows_distinct(columns_subset=["session_id"])
    .interrogate()
)
```


::: {.callout-note}
## Choosing the right key comes up again and again

Deciding which columns identify a record is something you will do repeatedly in this book. The
`columns_subset=` of `rows_complete()` names the fields a record cannot do without, and a
segmentation key names the groups you want results split by. In each case the question is the same:
which columns does this rule apply to? Getting that right is often more of the work than choosing
the method.
:::

## Row completeness

A null in a required field can break a calculation, drop rows from a join, or skew an aggregate.
The `rows_complete()` method checks completeness row by row, asking whether each row has everything
it needs. That is different from `col_vals_not_null()` in @sec-column-validations, which checks one
column at a time. Use `rows_complete()` when what matters is whether the record as a whole is
usable.

### Checking whole-row completeness

With no arguments, `rows_complete()` requires every column in a row to have a value and fails any
row with a null anywhere. Column `c` of `small_table` has two missing values, so those two rows
fail.

```{python}
(
    pb.Validate(data=small_table)
    .rows_complete()
    .interrogate()
)
```


### Completeness on required fields

The `columns_subset=` argument limits the check to the columns that must have values, so the
optional columns can contain nulls. If only columns `a`, `b`, and `d` of `small_table` are required,
and `c` is optional, every row passes.

```{python}
(
    pb.Validate(data=small_table)
    .rows_complete(columns_subset=["a", "b", "d"])
    .interrogate()
)
```


## Combining distinctness and completeness

The two checks work well together. With both in one plan, you can say that every record has its
required fields and that no two records share a key. The plan below does this for `game_revenue`.

```{python}
(
    pb.Validate(data=game_revenue, tbl_name="game_revenue", label="Row contract")
    .rows_distinct(columns_subset=["session_id", "time"])
    .rows_complete(columns_subset=["player_id", "session_id", "session_start"])
    .interrogate()
)
```

The completeness step passes for every row, while the distinctness step flags the same 22 rows we
saw earlier. Together they say the records are complete, but a few of them share a session and
timestamp and need a closer look. Pairing a uniqueness check on the key with a completeness check
on the required fields is also the basis of the data contracts in @sec-data-contracts.

## Beyond distinctness and completeness

Distinctness and completeness are the row checks you will use most, but other checks also look at
whole rows. When a rule involves several columns at once, such as a ship date that must come after
the order date unless the order was cancelled, the `conjointly()` method can express it. The
`specially()` method and the expression-based `col_vals_expr()` handle anything that does not fit
a built-in method. All three are covered in @sec-advanced-validation. When the judgment is about
meaning, such as whether a free-text review expresses a clear sentiment, the `prompt()` method
sends each row to a language model, as described in @sec-semantic-validation.

Both methods in this chapter also accept the same `segments=` and `pre=` arguments as the column
checks. The `segments=` argument gives a separate result for each group, as described in
@sec-segmented-validation. The `pre=` argument transforms or filters the data before the check
runs, which is handy for limiting a rule to the rows it applies to, such as requiring unique email
addresses only among active customers. @sec-advanced-validation covers `pre=` in full.

## Summary

Row validations catch problems that column checks cannot, because they look at the whole record.
The `rows_distinct()` method checks uniqueness, either across entire rows or, more usefully, across
a `columns_subset=` that defines the key. Every copy of a duplicated row counts as a failure, so the
failure count shows the full extent of the problem. Choosing the key is the main decision. Adding
columns one at a time and watching the failure count fall helps separate expected repetition from
real duplicates.

The `rows_complete()` method checks that values are present, either in every column or in a
`columns_subset=` that lists the required fields. Used together, the two checks state that records
are both complete and unique. The next chapter, @sec-table-validations, moves from rows to the table
as a whole, with checks on structure such as the schema, the table's dimensions, and how recent the
data is.
